notes: What to watch for: each narrative sets one or two expectations, things that should follow if its join is right, each with a date. Every later edition's writer checks the open ones against that day's headlines: kept or failed only with a headline behind it, otherwise open. Past its date an open expectation is closed by the site as failed.
Items are added and settled, never removed or reworded. Read the count beside each narrative's stated firmness: it is the site's own record of whether its confidence means anything.

items.line: Taiwan's fastest growth in fifty years rests on AI spending, so when US tech shares fall its state funds and central bank step in.
items.what: Taiwan's National Stabilization Fund or central bank reports further buying of shares or Taiwan dollars during November.
items.because: If Taiwan's market is now tied to doubts about US AI spending, further falls in US tech should bring further Taiwanese state action, not a single week's support.

items.line: Taiwan's fastest growth in fifty years rests on AI spending, so when US tech shares fall its state funds and central bank step in.
items.what: South Korea's government or a state fund announces support for chip shares or the won as tech stocks fall.
items.because: The join says chip-supplying economies now carry AI risk on public books, and South Korea is the other large supplier exposed to the same spending.

items.line: With oil near $118, the war's price rise is now argued over in wage talks, while governments cut fuel and sales taxes to slow it.
items.what: A national strike or wage settlement in a European country is reported with fuel or energy prices named among its reasons.
items.because: If the war's price rise has moved from the pump into pay, the next large pay disputes should cite it, which neither the oil price nor any single wage round predicts alone.

items.line: With oil near $118, the war's price rise is now argued over in wage talks, while governments cut fuel and sales taxes to slow it.
items.what: Japan's Diet passes the consumption tax reduction bill.
items.because: If governments are still choosing to absorb the price rise through tax rather than leave it to wages, Japan's bill should pass rather than stall.

items.line: More than four years into the invasion, European ministers shun Russia while Washington and African governments negotiate with it.
items.what: The US Treasury lifts or eases sanctions on a named Russian official, company or fund.
items.because: If Washington is treating Russia as a negotiating partner while Europe isolates it, the reported overture on sanctions should become an act that Europe does not copy.

items.line: More than four years into the invasion, European ministers shun Russia while Washington and African governments negotiate with it.
items.what: A European government or the EU publicly objects to a US step to ease Russia sanctions or to the terms of the Abu Dhabi talks.
items.because: The join predicts that the gap between European isolation and American bargaining becomes an open dispute between allies, not only a difference of tone.

items.line: Protests called for the same weekend in several European countries are met with bans in some cities and negotiation in others.
items.what: Organisers in two or more European countries announce a shared date for a further protest in November.
items.because: If these are one wave rather than local grievances that happened to meet on a weekend, the next call should again be made across borders.

items.line: Protests called for the same weekend in several European countries are met with bans in some cities and negotiation in others.
items.what: A European government proposes new limits on face coverings or on public gatherings, citing the 31 October protests.
items.because: The join is about how states set the limits of assembly, and a wave across countries should produce a rule rather than only one day's policing decision.
